chapter_title: Day 1: Istanbul, a City on Two Continents
learning_objective: The learner will classify fourteen foods found in Istanbul by the historical layer they came from, classifying at least 11 of 14 correctly on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** food-history-layers-sorter
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Understand
**Bloom Verb:** classify
**Learning Objective:** The learner will classify fourteen foods found in Istanbul by the historical layer they came from, classifying at least 11 of 14 correctly on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** food as history, Columbian Exchange, kaymak, Turkic herders, Rize (all defined in the section "Food as History" above). **Evidence of Mastery:** For each of fourteen food cards, the learner places the card in one of five layers and the placement is checked immediately. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct layer column in Content. Mastery is 11 of 14 correct on the first attempt. Reading the layer descriptions is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) Tomatoes and peppers have always been part of Mediterranean cooking. (2) Tea is an ancient Ottoman drink. (3) Turkish cooking is essentially the same as Arab cooking. (4) Everything on a Turkish table came with the Turks from Central Asia. (5) Coffee was always part of life in Istanbul. **Instructional Rationale:** Classifying foods by origin makes the learner apply the "where did it first grow and who brought it" questions to items they will actually eat. Immediate feedback with a reason turns each card into a short history lesson, and the mix of familiar and surprising items exposes the misconception that a food's familiarity means it is old. **Content:** The five layers, shown as labeled bins with these descriptions: 1. Ancient Mediterranean and Anatolia: grown or caught here since long before Byzantium. 2. Turkic herders from Central Asia: brought by Turkish-speaking herders who moved into Anatolia after 1071. 3. Ottoman trade and court: arrived through the empire's trade routes and palace kitchens, often from the Arab and Persian worlds. 4. The Americas, after 1492: arrived through the Columbian Exchange. 5. The Turkish Republic, after 1923: a 20th-century change. | # | Food card | Correct layer | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Olives and olive oil | 1 | Olive trees have been cultivated around the eastern Mediterranean for thousands of years. | | 2 | Bonito and bluefish from the Bosphorus | 1 | Greek Byzantium grew rich salting and exporting the fish that migrate through the strait. | | 3 | Chickpeas | 1 | Chickpeas were first farmed in what is now southeastern Turkey, thousands of years before the Greeks arrived. | | 4 | Yogurt | 2 | Yogurt is a Turkic word, and souring milk was how herders on the move kept it from spoiling. | | 5 | Ayran (salted yogurt drink) | 2 | A herders' drink made from yogurt and water, now Turkey's everyday drink with kebab. | | 6 | Kaymak (clotted cream) | 2 | Kaymak is a Turkic word for a herders' dairy food, eaten at breakfast with honey. | | 7 | Mantı (tiny meat dumplings with yogurt) | 2 | Dumplings came west with Turkic and Mongol peoples across the Central Asian steppe. | | 8 | Coffee | 3 | Coffee came up the Red Sea from Yemen, and the first coffeehouses opened in Istanbul in the 1550s. | | 9 | Pilaf (pilav) | 3 | Pilav is a Persian word; rice pilaf was a dish of the Persian and Ottoman courts. | | 10 | Şerbet (sweet fruit drink) | 3 | Şerbet comes from an Arabic word for a drink; the Ottoman court served it cooled with mountain snow. | | 11 | Tomatoes | 4 | Tomatoes came from the Americas and became common in Ottoman cooking only in the 1800s. | | 12 | Pul biber (red pepper flakes) | 4 | All chili peppers are American plants that reached the Ottoman Empire after 1492. | | 13 | Corn (mısır) roasted on a street cart | 4 | Corn is American; its Turkish name, mısır, also means Egypt, the route by which it arrived. | | 14 | Black tea (çay) | 5 | Turks drank coffee until the 20th century; tea plantations at Rize on the Black Sea date from the 1930s and 1940s. | **Provenance:** All origins and dates are from this chapter's sections "Food as History," "Turkish Cuisine," "Turkish Tea" and "Turkish Coffee," which follow standard food histories of the region. **Rules:** Each card has exactly one correct layer. Cards are presented one at a time in a shuffled order that is the same for every learner (seed 1453). A card counts as correct only on the learner's first placement; after feedback the card moves to its correct layer. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner sees the five layer bins with their descriptions and the first food card. 2. The learner places the card in a bin. The placement is marked correct or incorrect, the Why text appears, and the card settles into its correct bin. 3. The learner continues through all fourteen cards. 4. At the end, the learner sees all five bins filled, with the cards in each, and a score. 5. The learner should notice that the breakfast table they will eat on Day 2 includes cards from four different layers. **Feedback:** Fourteen cards, one attempt each. Correct: "Right: belongs to ." plus the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite: belongs to ." plus the Why text. A running score "Layers read: n of 14" is shown. At the end: "11 or more: you can read a menu like a history book" or "Fewer than 11: reread 'Food as History' and try again." A Restart button clears the bins and starts over in the same order. **Starting State:** Five empty bins with their descriptions, the first card showing, and the question "When did this food arrive on Istanbul's table?" **Chapter Anchors:** Turkic herders arrived after 1071. The Columbian Exchange began after 1492. Tomatoes common in Ottoman cooking only from the 1800s. First Istanbul coffeehouses in the 1550s. Rize tea plantations in the 1930s and 1940s. Mısır means both corn and Egypt.
